changes.text: Pages now know what links to them. When your assistant reads a page it also sees the pages that point at it, so it can follow a thread in both directions.

Search can now find a page by what it means, not only by its words. A question that shares no word with the page that answers it can still find that page. This works once the people who run a reef switch on its own embedding service. Until then, and whenever that service is slow, search works by words as before. A search with a quoted phrase or a `-word` stays exact.

The privacy page now says how search reads your pages: two models that reef runs itself turn them into search vectors and order the results. Your text goes to no other company, and the models do not learn from it.

Search can now read its best results again next to your question, and put the one that answers it first. This works once the people who run a reef switch on its own reranking service. Until then, and whenever that service is slow, search keeps the order it had.
Search now understands Dutch word forms as well as English ones, so "contract" finds a page that says "contracten". Searching is also faster.

Reef now says "space" where it said "cove" and "engram" where it said "page". Your notes and spaces are the same; only the words changed. Your assistant now has 16 clear tools instead of 31. It can ask a question of your memory, get a brief before a session, or add an entry to a log. Setups you already have keep working: when an assistant uses an old tool, Reef tells it which new one to use. Reload your assistant's tool list once to see the new tools. Creating, renaming and leaving spaces, and inviting people, now happen on the website only. The Claude Code plugin and the command-line tool get a new major version. Update both.
Search now finds a page even when it does not contain every word you typed. Pages with all of your words still come first, and questions in ordinary language find far more.

reef can keep a private log of what you search for, to measure and improve search. It is switched off, and it starts only after you have been told. Only you can see your searches, and each one is deleted after 90 days. The privacy page now also lists the record of which pages you open.
When you ask a question, stored files no longer crowd out the pages that answer it. A search for a name or a few words still finds the file first.
The member list of a shared cove works again, on the website and for your assistant. Sharing a page with a cove works again too: it shows who will see it, and that list failed to load.
Pages now show when they last changed, not when they were made. Existing pages were corrected to the time of their latest edit.
The privacy page now says that the search log is on. It has been on since 18 November 2026.
Every public page now credits rugvin, with the fin mark visible on touchscreens as well as on hover or keyboard focus.

The app looks quieter and easier to scan. Each cove's creature is now drawn large enough to recognise, pages and settings sit on their own cards, and headings no longer compete with the text beneath them.
The operating protocol and tool descriptions now illustrate themselves with plainly fictional examples instead of page names borrowed from one real reef.
Your assistant now receives the operating protocol and your persona the moment it loads the memory index, instead of needing a second call it could forget to make.
Bulk-loading the whole corpus for maintenance now also hands your assistant the operating protocol and persona, so no entry point delivers your memory without its rules.

Your assistant now treats reef as the record when its own built-in memory disagrees — it tells you both sides instead of quietly picking one, and writes down whichever answer you settle on. Assistants limited to search and fetch, like ChatGPT connectors outside developer mode, are now offered the operating protocol as the first search result, so they arrive knowing how to read and write your memory too.

A new reef mark now actually reaches your assistant. The icon was advertised at a fixed address, so a client that had already fetched one was entitled to keep showing it; each release now points at a fresh address instead.

reef now has documentation at reefwith.me/docs — how coves and pages work, how your assistant reads and writes memory, the steps to connect Claude, ChatGPT, Codex or the CLI, and every tool listed in one place. Search it from the panel on the left, or jump straight to a section and share the link.
reef now works in clients that only allow two tools — ChatGPT connectors outside developer mode, and company-knowledge sources — by answering to `search` and `fetch` alongside its full set.
reef now says plainly that it is free while it is small, and that you will hear about any change from us rather than from a bill.
Reef now uses a compact branching brain-coral mark across the app and its icons, with a more detailed companion mark on the landing page.
Reef now uses its curled brain-coral mark everywhere, including the app, website, favicons, shared previews, and assistant connections.

Everything reef calls a shared memory is now a cove, in the app, the tools your assistant uses, and the CLI. If you have scripts or saved prompts that name a space — `list_spaces`, a `space` argument, `reef list-spaces` — they need the cove spelling now.
Storing a large file no longer fails: uploads up to the full 25MB file limit now make it through, where anything over about 3MB used to be rejected before reef saw it.

Install reef in Claude Code with two commands, and get `/reef:recall`, `/reef:remember` and `/reef:whats-new` alongside it. Your assistant also asks before anything that would overwrite or delete something, and stops asking to read.
Reef now uses its new brain-fan mark everywhere, from the app and website to favicons, social previews, and assistant connections.
The new brain-fan mark is now better balanced with the landing-page headline and navigation.

Inviting someone into a cove now reminds you that reef sends no email, so nothing reaches them until you pass the message on yourself. Previously the invite just reported success and the person you invited was never told.
The brain-fan mark now has clear edge space and a better-balanced size across reef's site, app, and shared previews.
The reef landing page now tells its story through a shared-memory conversation, clearer sections, and a shorter path to setup.
Links to reef now unfurl properly — share one in a chat, a post or a message and it arrives as a card instead of a bare address. The changelog has moved to reefwith.me/changelog.

While places are open for the launch, the reef home page now says so and invites you to take one. Once they're gone it goes back to explaining that you get in when someone already on reef invites you.
The reef website’s hero mark now has a richer seafoam-to-deep-teal gradient in both light and dark mode.

Connecting an assistant now shows reef's own approval page. Before you approve, it names where your sign-in will land and spells out plainly what a connected assistant can reach: everything you can read, write and manage in your coves.
The reef mark on the landing page now stands cleanly on the background without a decorative shape cutting across its base.
The reef website background now stays calm and clear without oversized decorative arcs competing with the content.
The reef website now carries its underwater character throughout, with gentle texture, currents, and more dimensional coves in light and dark mode.
reef can now tell you what's changed since you last looked. Open "What's new" from the account menu to see it.
reef now has terms of service, linked from every page's footer alongside the privacy policy and a changelog that actually opens.
